narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to evolve with a renewed focus on embracing natural textures. The resurgence of the Natural Hair Movement encouraged individuals to ditch chemical treatments and instead celebrate their afro-textured hair. Styles like the Afro, which was created by combing out natural growth or using chemical curling products, became increasingly popular. Dreadlocks, also known as locs, were another style that gained traction during this time. Protective hairstyles, such as Bantu knots and box braids, remained a staple in many African cultures, serving not only as a fashion statement but also as a way to minimize hair breakage and protect against environmental damage. While the Jheri curl may have been a relic of the past, these styles represented a new era of self-expression and identity for Black and African women, who were unapologetically embracing their natural beauty.
